content.text: The Power of Many: Collaboration at Scale

Computing and the Internet have made it possible to connect millions of people around the world and harness their collective knowledge, effort, and resources in ways that were never before possible. Topic 5.4 is about how widespread access to information and public data enables people to collaborate at massive scale to solve problems, conduct research, and fund ideas. This is crowdsourcing — and it has fundamentally changed how humans solve problems together.
Widespread Access Enables Problem-Solving at Scale

content.term: How does widespread access to data enable problem solving?
content.definition: Widespread access to information and public data facilitates the identification of problems, development of solutions, and dissemination of results. This enables crowdsourcing and citizen science at a large scale.

content.text: Before the Internet, identifying a problem often required expensive surveys or research by professionals. Solving it required coordinating specialists in person. Sharing results required publishing in journals accessible only to other specialists. The Internet changed all three — anyone with a computing device can now participate in finding problems, contributing solutions, and sharing results with the world. This is what enables crowdsourcing and citizen science at a scale that was previously impossible.

rows: Identifying problems required expensive professional surveys or research
Anyone can identify and report problems through online platforms — millions of observations replace a few professional ones
Developing solutions required coordinating specialists in the same location
People worldwide can collaborate on solutions simultaneously regardless of location
Disseminating results required professional publication accessible to few
Results can be shared instantly with anyone in the world through websites, data repositories, and social platforms
Funding required convincing banks or wealthy investors
Crowdfunding connects ideas directly with thousands of small contributors

content.definition: The practice of obtaining input or information from a large number of people via the Internet. Offers new models for collaboration such as connecting businesses or social causes with funding. Human capabilities can be enhanced by collaboration via computing.

content.text: Crowdsourcing is the practice of obtaining input or information from a large number of people via the Internet. The 'crowd' does the work — contributing data, money, ideas, or effort — and the organizer aggregates and uses those contributions. The result is that tasks that would be impossibly large for any individual or small team become achievable through the combined effort of many.

rows: Crowdfunding
Money — small contributions from many people fund a project, business, or cause
Kickstarter: thousands of backers each contribute $20-$100 to fund a new product that no single investor would back
Crowdsourced data
Observations or data points collected from many distributed contributors
Waze: millions of drivers report road conditions, accidents, and speed traps — collectively building a real-time traffic map
Crowdsourced knowledge
Information, expertise, or written content from many contributors
Wikipedia: millions of volunteer editors collectively write and maintain an encyclopedia larger than any professional team could create
Crowdsourced labor
Small amounts of work from many people that collectively complete a large task
Online platforms where thousands of volunteers tag images, transcribe documents, or identify patterns in data
Crowdsourced ideas
Creative solutions or feedback from a large population
Online platforms where users vote on and suggest product features or solutions to design challenges

content.definition:
Crowdsourcing: obtaining input or information from a large number of people via the Internet — broader than just science, includes funding, ideas, and data.
Citizen Science: specifically scientific research conducted by distributed non-scientists who contribute data using their own devices. Citizen science is a form of crowdsourcing applied to scientific research.

Scientific research conducted in whole or in part by distributed individuals, many of whom may not be scientists, who contribute relevant data using their own computing devices. A form of crowdsourcing applied to scientific research.

content.text: Citizen science is crowdsourcing applied specifically to scientific research. Non-scientists contribute real scientific data using their own computing devices — smartphones, computers, and sensors — enabling research that professional scientists could never conduct alone. Science has been affected by using distributed and citizen science to solve scientific problems. The scale and geographic distribution of citizen scientists allows data collection across time and space that would be impossible for any research team.

rows: Bird population tracking (eBird)
Amateur birdwatchers log bird sightings using a smartphone app from locations worldwide
Millions of data points reveal migration patterns, population changes, and habitat shifts across entire continents
Galaxy classification (Galaxy Zoo)
Volunteers look at telescope images and classify galaxy shapes
Tasks that would take one astronomer centuries are completed in months — humans outperform computers at shape recognition
Air quality monitoring
People with low-cost sensors on their homes or phones report local air quality
Fine-grained air quality maps reveal pollution hot spots that a few government sensors would miss
Medical data contribution
People use apps to log symptoms, activity, and health data over time
Large longitudinal health data sets enable research on chronic conditions that clinical trials cannot capture
Earthquake detection (MyShake)
Smartphones detect vibrations and report to a central server
A global network of millions of phones can detect earthquakes faster than traditional seismic sensor networks

content.label: Key Idea
content.text: Science has been affected by using distributed and citizen science to solve scientific problems. Citizen science is not just 'helping scientists' — it has fundamentally changed what scientific research is possible. Data sets that would be impossible for any professional team to collect are now routinely assembled through citizen science. This represents a genuine transformation in how science is done.

content.term: How widespread access to data enables problem solving
content.definition: Widespread access to information and public data facilitates the identification of problems, development of solutions, and dissemination of results — enabling crowdsourcing and citizen science at a large scale.

content.text: Human capabilities can be enhanced by collaboration via computing. Individual humans have limited time, attention, geographic reach, and expertise. When computing connects many people, their combined capabilities far exceed what any individual or small team could achieve. This is not just about doing existing tasks faster — it enables entirely new kinds of tasks that no previous human collaboration model could accomplish.

rows: One person can visit a few locations to observe wildlife
Millions of citizen scientists collectively cover every habitat on Earth simultaneously
One team can review thousands of research papers
Crowdsourced review platforms enable communities to collectively evaluate millions of papers
One entrepreneur can pitch to a handful of investors
Crowdfunding platforms connect ideas with millions of potential backers worldwide
One programmer can write and test a program alone
Open source communities with thousands of contributors produce software used by billions

content.text: Crowdsourcing offers new models for collaboration, such as connecting businesses or social causes with funding. Before crowdfunding platforms, a new business needed to convince a bank or a venture capitalist to provide startup capital. A social cause needed to fundraise through events or direct mail. Now, either can reach millions of potential supporters directly and collect small contributions from each — together adding up to substantial funding.

rows: Startup funding: convince one or a few large investors to provide capital
Crowdfunding: thousands of small backers each contribute — startup is funded without giving control to any single investor
Scientific research: funded by government grants to professional researchers
Citizen science: research conducted by millions of volunteers with their own devices — cost near zero
Encyclopedia: written by professional editors at a publisher
Wikipedia: written and maintained by millions of volunteers — constantly updated, free to access
Product design: company pays professional designers
Open innovation: public contest invites solutions from millions — best ideas surface regardless of who had them

content.label: Exam Tip
content.text: Know the distinction between crowdsourcing and citizen science: crowdsourcing is the broader concept (obtaining input from many people via the Internet — includes funding, data, knowledge, labor). Citizen science is specifically scientific research conducted by distributed non-scientists using their own computing devices. Citizen science IS a form of crowdsourcing — but not all crowdsourcing is citizen science.
Summary: What to Know for the Exam

items: Widespread access to information and public data facilitates identification of problems, development of solutions, and dissemination of results
Crowdsourcing is the practice of obtaining input or information from a large number of people via the Internet
Crowdsourcing offers new models for collaboration such as connecting businesses or social causes with funding
Human capabilities can be enhanced by collaboration via computing
Citizen science is scientific research conducted by distributed individuals, many of whom may not be scientists, who contribute relevant data using their own computing devices
Science has been affected by using distributed and citizen science to solve scientific problems
Citizen science IS a form of crowdsourcing — applied specifically to scientific research
Crowdsourcing is broader — it includes funding, data collection, knowledge creation, and labor, not just science
